source.title: The Unlocking Spell on Base LLMs: Rethinking Alignment via In-Context Learning
source.authors: Bill Yuchen Lin; Abhilasha Ravichander; Ximing Lu; Nouha Dziri; Melanie Sclar; Khyathi Raghavi Chandu; Chandra Bhagavatula; Ye-Jin Choi

record.tranche_reason: The study directly compares token distributions from base and alignment-tuned models, including per-position KL divergence, but uses token-rank and distribution-shift analysis rather than the original study’s method.
record.gate_note: The study tests whether distribution shifts are concentrated earlier in responses (V3). It does not fine-tune models on harmful or benign examples, test compliant-token prefilling or other bypasses, localize safety to weights, identify a causal source of shallowness, or test methods for deepening safety. Its U RIAL safety evaluations use a deliberately safety-oriented system prompt and demonstrations, so they are not evidence about uninduced safety behavior or the claim versions.
record.test_reason: It measures per-position KL, base rank and base probability between base and aligned models along aligned-model responses, which is the V3 quantity. But it averages over 1,000 mostly benign prompts (800 helpfulness, 200 red-team), not harmful prompts alone, and uses different templates for the base and aligned models.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that alignment changes a small fraction of token choices (about 5–8% shifted), mainly stylistic tokens and safety disclaimers. They find it matters more for early than late tokens, and that base models already hold the needed knowledge. They show that tuning-free ICL (URIAL) can match or beat SFT/RLHF on strong base models.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes base-versus-aligned token distributions with rank, probability, and KL measures; it does not use harmful-example fine-tuning or compliant-opening bypass experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured shift varies by response position; the paper also uses different input templates for base and aligned models.

fits_no_version.finding: Alignment changes the top token at only about 5–8% of positions. Shifted tokens are mostly stylistic or refusal/safety tokens ('cannot', 'sorry', 'apolog', 'However').
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment's token-level changes are sparse and concentrated in stylistic and refusal tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: Base models given an in-context safety prompt plus 3 examples reach safety scores close to the aligned models' (e.g. Llama-2-7b 1.57 zero-shot vs 4.29 URIAL vs 5.00 chat). This is induced by the prompt.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety behaviour of aligned models can be largely reproduced by prompting base models, without tuning.

record.problems: The study notes that the base and aligned models receive different templates. Per-position KL trends are described without numerical values or uncertainty estimates; some pairwise token-rank percentages are shown only in a figure.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results omitted. URIAL’s safety ratings and examples were not extracted as claim rows because the prompt and demonstrations deliberately induce safety-oriented responses and do not test the listed fine-tuning or bypass interventions.

untested.parts: Harmful prompts alone, with per-position KL values given as numbers. Which model pair Figure 4 uses.
All: no prefilling, suffix or decoding bypass test.
All: no causal test of the source of shallowness.

missing.what: Per-position KL, base rank and base probability curves, which are plotted but have no numbers in the text and no stated model pair.

record.verdict_notes: This paper predates the original source and shows a positional trend that the original builds on, but over general rather than harmful prompts. The differing base and aligned templates may inflate early-position KL. The URIAL safety scores are induced by a safety prompt and were correctly kept out of the claim rows.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful fine-tuning intervention or harmful-request compliance rate.
No benign fine-tuning intervention or harmful-request compliance rate.
Does not report numerical per-position KL values or isolate harmful prompts; it reports qualitative per-position trends and aggregate token-rank results.
No compliant-opening prefilling, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change bypass test.
No parameter or rank localization test.
No causal test of whether training data or objective produces shallowness.
No safety-deepening intervention or evaluation of whether it holds up.

rows.subject: Llama-2-7b-chat
rows.operation_detail: Rank aligned-model output tokens under the base model’s next-token distribution.
rows.measure: Share of aligned response tokens at base rank 1, ranks 2–3, and rank greater than 3.
rows.note: The figure gives 77.7%, 14.5%, and 7.8%, respectively. These aggregate shares do not by themselves show how the shift varies by response position.
rows.check: An aggregate share of unshifted, marginal and shifted tokens (77.7/14.5/7.8%) with no position breakdown, so it cannot show where the shift sits. It is related to how shallow alignment is but does not measure V3. The values appear in the Figure 3 labels, so 'figure only' understates them.

rows.subject: Base and aligned LLMs (pair not stated for this figure)
rows.operation_detail: Measure per-position KL divergence between base and aligned next-token distributions during decoding.
rows.value: KL divergence goes down over time; later positions have less distribution shift than earlier positions.
rows.note: The paper describes the plotted trend but does not provide numerical KL values.
rows.check: The model pair for Figure 4 is not stated. The prompt set is a mixed benign/red-team set, not harmful prompts alone. The trend is described in words only, with no numbers, and KL is computed under different base and aligned templates.

source_check.locator_found: Section 2.2, Figure 4 and accompanying paragraph, pp. 4–5; Section 4.1; Appendix C.

rows.subject: Base and aligned LLMs (pair not stated for this figure)
rows.operation_detail: Measure the base-model rank of each token selected by the aligned model during decoding.
rows.measure: Average base rank of aligned-model output tokens.
rows.value: Average base rank is lower than 5 soon after t ≥ 5.
rows.note: The authors interpret this as aligned-model top tokens usually being among the base model’s top five after the early positions.
rows.check: The model pair is not stated and the prompts are mixed. The text says average base rank drops below 5 'soon after t ≥ 5', which is consistent with the shift sitting in the first few positions.

rows.subject: Base and aligned LLMs (pair not stated for this figure)

rows.measure: Base-model probability of aligned-model output tokens.
rows.value: The base probability can be close to 1.0 toward the end.
rows.note: The reported trend supports smaller distribution shifts at later response positions.
rows.check: The model pair is not stated and the prompts are mixed. This is an indirect proxy (base probability of the aligned token) and its trend is described qualitatively.

relationships.reason: KL falls and base probability rises over positions, and base rank drops below 5 after about t=5 (r4–r6). This is shown only qualitatively and not on harmful prompts alone.
relationships.display_finding: KL fell and base-model probability rose across positions, and base rank dropped below 5 after about position 5. This is shown qualitatively and not for harmful prompts on their own.
